gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much gain the Fluance RT81 and RT81+ built-in preamps add. From Fluance's own figures it is about 32 dB on the RT81 (140 mV out from a 3.5 mV cartridge) and about 31 dB on the RT81+ (140 mV from 4.0 mV). Both decks put out the same 140 mV (−17 dBV) line signal, so the $50 step up to the RT81+ does not make it play louder through powered speakers.
standout_why: I compared three pages. Valve & Vinyl (valveandvinyl.com/turntables/crosley-alternatives) gives 36 dB nominal gain for the Audio-Technica decks, but for the RT81 it says only 'Switchable, with true bypass; no gain figure' and lists no output voltage for any deck. Platter & Plinth (platterandplinth.com/turntables/best-with-preamp) lists no output level or gain for the RT81 or RT81+; its only gain figure is the Sony PS-LX3BT's −4/0/+6 dB switch. The fewbetter.com result is off-topic: the page has no turntables at all. None of them gives a line-output voltage, a gain figure for the Fluance decks, or the fact that the RT81 and RT81+ put out the same level.
decides: This backs ChatGPT's RT81 pick on value. The RT81+ costs $50 more ($349.99 vs $299.99) for a better AT-VM95E cartridge and the AT-VMN95E stylus line, not for a stronger signal into powered speakers. Both put out 140 mV, which is 7 dB below the common −10 dBV (316 mV) consumer line level, so a shopper using either one in LINE mode should expect to turn the speakers up more than for a phone or streamer. I could not compare against the AT-LP70X or the Sony because I couldn't open their maker spec pages.
